lesson.title: Sliding Nucleosomes to Open or Close a Gene
lesson.summary: Chromatin remodeling complexes use energy from ATP to physically slide, reposition, or eject nucleosomes, exposing or hiding stretches of DNA for the transcription machinery.
lesson.body:
DNA methylation and histone modification, covered in the previous two sections, both work by attaching chemical tags: a methyl group on a base, an acetyl or methyl group on a histone tail. Chromatin remodeling is different in kind. Rather than adding a chemical tag, it is a mechanical process: large protein complexes physically grab hold of nucleosomes and move them.

These ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complexes, of which the SWI/SNF family is a well-studied example, use energy released from breaking down ATP to slide a nucleosome along the DNA, loosen the contacts between DNA and the histone core, evict a histone octamer from the DNA entirely, or swap in a specialized variant histone. The functional result is a change in physical accessibility: a promoter or enhancer that was wrapped tightly around a nucleosome, and therefore hidden from transcription factors and RNA polymerase, can be exposed once the nucleosome is repositioned. The same machinery can work in reverse, sliding a nucleosome onto a previously exposed regulatory sequence to cover it up and shut a gene down.

This process happens inside the nucleus, where all of a cell's chromatin is housed, and it works hand in hand with histone modification. A common pattern is that an acetylated or otherwise modified histone tail acts as a docking site, recruiting a chromatin remodeling complex to that specific location, so the chemical mark and the physical repositioning reinforce each other rather than acting independently.

Because correctly opening and closing the right genes at the right time is essential for normal development and normal cell function, defects in chromatin remodeling complexes are linked to a number of developmental disorders and cancers. With chromatin remodeling, the survey of DNA and chromatin based epigenetic mechanisms is complete: DNA methylation, histone modification, and chromatin remodeling. Not every layer of gene regulation touches DNA or chromatin, though. The next section turns to a different strategy entirely, one that acts on messenger RNA after a gene has already been transcribed.
